title: The Omer: a trait a week
hookLine: seven weeks, seven traits: love, strength, balance, endurance, humility, foundation, presence
tomorrow: why read one name, when there are so many?

cards: Countdown apps are for things you're waiting for: a trip, a birthday, the last day of school. The Torah sets a count-up instead.
It starts during Passover and runs to the next festival, Shavuot: seven weeks, counted out loud, one night at a time. Counting what? In the Torah, days and weeks toward a harvest offering.
Later, the Kabbalists gave each week a second job: one trait of the heart, worked on like a muscle, while ordinary life keeps happening around you.

teach.b: Leviticus gives the count: "And ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the day of rest, from the day that ye brought the sheaf of the waving; seven weeks shall there be complete."

teach.h: THE OMER: A SHEAF OF BARLEY.
teach.b: The sheaf is the omer, a measure of new barley brought as an offering, and the season carries its name. Those who keep the count say a blessing each night and the number: today is so many days of the Omer.
Then the mystics added a map.

The Kabbalists linked each week to a quality from their teaching about how God's light reaches the world: chesed, love; gevurah, strength and limits; tiferet, balance; netzach, endurance; hod, humility; yesod, foundation; malchut, presence.
Inside each week, every day pairs the week's trait with another, so one night is love within strength, another humility within love. You don't need the whole map to use it.
Take the week's trait as a lens for whatever the week hands you: a fight, a deadline, someone in the hospital.
Love week asks, what's the kind move here? Strength week asks, where's the line? A calendar becomes a slow course in character, ending at the festival of receiving the Torah.

how: Jews who count the Omer say a blessing and the day's number each night from Passover to Shavuot; some also follow the Kabbalists' map of seven traits, one for each week.

games.q: week two of the Omer: gevurah, strength and limits. a friend asks you to cover her shift again, the fourth time this month. what does this week's trait ask?
o: where's the line: say no kindly, and mean it.
love always says yes, so cover it once more.
nothing; the traits are just labels for the nights.
games.why: gevurah is strength and limits. love week asks for the kind move; strength week asks where the line is. the same situation, a different lens.

practice: Say a trait out loud, once, slowly: chesed, love, if you're starting at the beginning. Then name one person or one situation this week where you could use it, and say that out loud too.
End with one slow breath, and let the word settle.

wordCard.voice: The Omer: the seven weeks counted from Passover to Shavuot, named for a sheaf of barley, and walked one trait at a time.

orig.note: Hebrew: a sheaf, a measure of grain; the offering the count is named for.

carryVoice: A line for the week: a trait a week, counted one night at a time. That's today.
